case.question: Find advice about running customer interviews from guests other than Teresa Torres.
case.expected_behavior: Retrieve customer-research interview advice while respecting the Teresa Torres exclusion.
case.rubric: Use relevant non-Teresa advice; podcast-host interviews or job interviews alone do not satisfy customer interviews. Do not attribute excluded Teresa passages to another guest.

answer.summary: To set up consistent customer interviews, write a template email for yourself that you can send out easily, such as 'Hey, thank you so much for using the product.' and 'I would really love to hear about your experience so far and get your feedback.'

sections.heading: Tactical steps for setting up consistent customer interviews (email template, hypothesis, query, frequency)
sections.content: To set up consistent customer interviews, write a template email for yourself that you can send out easily, such as 'Hey, thank you so much for using the product.' and 'I would really love to hear about your experience so far and get your feedback.'

sections.heading: Heuristic for determining sufficient time spent talking to customers
sections.content: A heuristic for determining sufficient time spent talking to customers is to look at your calendar and ensure that 20-30% of your time is dedicated to customer meetings, calls, or meetings with customers.

sections.heading: Strategies for overcoming social anxiety and awkwardness when initiating customer conversations
sections.content: To overcome social anxiety and awkwardness when initiating customer conversations, you need to get past the feeling of looking stupid and start doing it until it doesn't feel bad anymore.

sections.heading: Methods to gain deep customer insight through observation and researcher collaboration
sections.content: To gain deep customer insight through observation and researcher collaboration, become best friends with a researcher, spend time watching customers use the product firsthand, and ask questions like 'How do I actually set up time with customers?' and 'How do I compensate them?'

sections.heading: System for automating continuous customer conversations for product teams
sections.content: A system for automating continuous customer conversations involves organizing your PMs, designers, engineering managers, and PMMs to constantly talk to customers by default, with customer conversations showing up on their calendar every week without them getting involved.

sections.heading: Building an opt-in database of customers for research participation
sections.content: To build an opt-in database of customers for research participation, make sure that you have customers aware that 'Hey, we might contact you to do customer interviews,' and 'Do you want to participate in alphas and betas?'

sections.heading: Criteria for selecting 'best customers' for research and using surveys as a precursor to interviews
sections.content: The criteria for selecting 'best customers' for research involve identifying those that get a ton of value from your product, pay, are happy, low-maintenance, and signed up for your product recently enough that they remember what life was like before.

S6.title: How to ask the right questions, project confidence, and win over skeptics | Paige Costello (Asana)
S6.text:
24:46):
In terms of knowing the insight and knowing thy customer, putting the time, I imagine, is a big element of that. Is that how you do that, or is there anything else along those lines that's just like, "Here's how I get really good at this?"

Paige Costello (00:24:59):
When you take a new role, become best friends with a researcher, and spend time watching customers use the product firsthand because what they maybe report on or are trying to do a study about might be very different from what you observe, but you really just need that front row seat with customers, and so asking, "How do I actually set up time with customers? How do I compensate them? How do I read the tickets?" Whatever. It's amazing how little you have to do to quickly catch up to understanding who the organization is solving for well and poorly, and how people really use your product versus how your teams use your product, especially in organizations where there are heavy dogfooding cultures. It's really risky to become less sensitive to the needs and behaviors of customers because people think they are their customer, and it also becomes very navel-gazey. So I think the more you get out and break up how people are having conversations about what we should do and why, and what we shouldn't do and why, and it's not about your opinion, it's about asking questions, and then bringing insight can really change the nature of the conversation and build trust.

S7.title: Picking sharp problems, increasing virality, and unique product frameworks | Oji Udezue (Typeform)
S7.text:
king to customers, another one of your big bullet points in the book is around continuous customer discovery, and I'm curious what you found to be successful in actually doing that. A lot of people talk about it when you keep talking to customers, get feedback constantly. What actually works in your experience?

Oji Udezue (00:31:34):
Yeah, I feel like all of park management is about discovery these days. Everyone talks about it, and I want to make a distinction. I think discovery is when you use customer conversations to understand a very specific thing that you want to optimize further workflow that you want to optimize further. And then you call the people who are most likely to be affected and you do use various research strategies to talk to them. There's a version of that also that is what I call continuous conversations, which is a Calendly and a Typeform, which we'll do more and more of. You should organize it so that your PMs, your designers, your engineering managers and your PMMs are constantly talking to customers by default. Meaning that customer conversations show up on their calendar every week automagically, without them getting involved. And then they're trained on how to have the conversation, because the death of customer discovery is friction. If you ask individuals to do customer discovery, they will not do customer discovery.
